title: GPCR antagonism via rewiring of receptor trafficking and degradation.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and opened all 6 files of the paper's Zenodo deposit (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21964503, 'GTAC', CC-BY-4.0, ~6 MB total): README.docx, PWS_ECORE.xlsx and four GraphPad Prism files (.prism). The README maps each file to figure panels. I unzipped the Prism files (they are ZIP archives of JSON sheets) and counted 375 data sheets in total (JO_RX_Nb 12, KR_RXFP1 35, KR_AT1R_Misc 54, LS_CCR6 274); each sheet is titled by figure panel (e.g. 'Figure 2b, Extended Data Figure 4c panel 1') and holds one small dose-response or bar-chart table with 3 replicate sub-columns, with the actual numbers held in Prism's internal dataset objects, not as a readable column. I opened PWS_ECORE.xlsx with pandas: 10 sheets, an Index sheet listing 9 data sheets with 4,410 / 58 / 4,000 / 53 / 66 / 42 / 33 / 84 / 39 rows, columns such as condition, arm, pre_median_ibi_s, post_median_ibi_s (cardiac-tissue beating measurements). I also pulled the PubMed Central (PMC) copy of the article (PMC13632652) and read its Data Availability statement verbatim.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The potency claims (one to two orders of magnitude better than conventional antibody antagonists), the receptor panel (BILF1, RXFP1, CCR6, AT1R, M3R) and the design rules for the degrader all come from the article text. Supplementary Tables 1-7 (9.4-14.5 KB .xlsx each) could not be retrieved: the article is not open access in Europe PMC (supplementaryFiles endpoint returns 'not open access'), and the PMC /bin/ links return an HTML challenge page instead of the spreadsheet, so I know only their listed sizes and the captions saying Tables 4-5 are image-analysis sample sizes and correlations, Table 6 qPCR primer sequences, Table 7 statistical p-values.

a1_downloadable.note: Zenodo record 21964503 is open, CC-BY-4.0, no login; I downloaded all 6 files (~6 MB). Only the journal's Supplementary Tables are paywalled.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL, verified in the files. There is no potency, EC50, DC50 or percent-degradation column anywhere. The deposit is figure source data: 375 GraphPad Prism sheets named after figure panels, each a raw dose-response block. Any label would have to be constructed by parsing a proprietary binary-ish format, re-fitting curves, and hand-mapping panel titles to antibody constructs.

a3_inputs_present.note: FAIL. Constructs appear only as short internal names in sheet titles ('RX002i4', 'LS13', 'A12', 'CCR6 Fab-Fc H31A'). No antibody sequences, no CDR definitions, no construct architecture table in the open deposit; those would be in the paywalled Supplementary Tables I could not open.

a4_units_stated.note: Where tabular data exists it is labelled with units: PWS_ECORE.xlsx columns are explicit (pre_median_ibi_s, t_rel_to_injection_s, mechanical_signal_au). Prism sheets carry axis titles per panel but no global units column.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL. The only machine-readable table (PWS_ECORE.xlsx) has 8,785 rows across 9 sheets, but these are time-series traces and per-spot summaries from a single cardiac-contractility experiment: the experimental units number 33-84 per sheet. The degrader data proper is 375 figure-panel sheets, i.e. on the order of tens of distinct antibody constructs tested, far under the ~1,500 (or ~400 classification) threshold.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Entire deposit is 6 MB; trivially fits in memory. Size is the one thing that is not a problem here.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The README.docx file-to-figure map matches the figure panel titles I found inside the Prism archives, and the PWS_ECORE Index sheet row counts match the actual sheet shapes I read with pandas.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels, where they exist, are direct wet-lab measurements (flow cytometry surface receptor levels, luciferase signalling, western blots, live-cell imaging, mouse plasma levels) - not another model's output. A8 is the one deep check this paper would have passed.

existing_models.name: DeepPROTACs (Nature Communications 2022) - a deep neural network that predicts whether a PROTAC (proteolysis-targeting chimera, a small molecule that drags a protein to the cell's disposal machinery) will degrade its target
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported 77.95% average accuracy and 0.847 AUROC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) on its test set; split details not verified by me, and it is trained on small-molecule PROTACs, not antibodies.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved - I only read the search abstract, not the discussion.

existing_models.name: DegradeMaster and a deep-learning plus quantitative-systems-pharmacology model for PROTAC DC50 (half-maximal degradation concentration), both surfaced in search
existing_models.score_and_split: One reports Pearson correlation 0.95 between predicted and observed Dmax (maximum degradation); split not verified by me.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (a protein language model with small CPU-runnable checkpoints) would be the natural backbone for antibody-arm sequences, but the sequences are not in the open data.
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU would be ample for the data volume here; the blocker is the number of examples, not compute.
backbone.licence: Data is CC-BY-4.0; ESM-2 is MIT-licensed. Licences are not the problem.

integration.partner_dataset: None usable. A join to UniProt (receptor accessions P21462 for a chemokine receptor and P11047, both text-mined from the article) or to PDB 4H11 would attach sequence and structure to the five receptors studied, but five rows is not a dataset.
integration.join_key: UniProt accession (receptor side only); no identifier exists for the antibody constructs.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Cannot be written honestly: with tens of constructs against five receptors, no join turns this into a question a model could answer.

controls.positive_control: None definable, because there is no feature/label table to run a control on.
controls.external_validation: A related public resource exists in principle (PROTAC-DB and the LYTAC/AbTAC literature), but it measures small-molecule degraders, not bispecific antibody degraders, so it is not a validation set for this assay.

honest_claim_h3: No honest model claim is available: with a few dozen bispecific antibody constructs measured across five receptors in one laboratory, any model would be describing this lab's design choices rather than predicting degradability.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a bispecific antibody's design to predict how much of a cell-surface receptor it removes.
plain_idea.train_on: What the model would have seen: for each engineered antibody, which receptor arm it uses, which transferrin-receptor arm, the valency and the geometry of the two arms. The verified number of such constructs is on the order of tens, not the thousands a model needs.
plain_idea.predict: How strongly the antibody lowers the receptor on the cell surface (potency and maximum knockdown), measured by flow cytometry, luciferase signalling assays and western blots in the authors' own cell lines.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: If it worked, antibody engineers could rank degrader designs before making them, which is the expensive step. Here it cannot be attempted, because the design-to-outcome pairs number in the tens and the outcomes live inside GraphPad Prism figure files rather than a table.

more_or_better_data.why: The published degradation models were trained on thousands of small-molecule PROTAC measurements (PROTAC-DB-scale). This deposit holds tens of antibody constructs, and in a format with no potency column.

confidence_score.why: Prism sheets do carry 3 replicates per concentration, which would in principle give a noise estimate, but with tens of constructs there is no basis for per-prediction confidence.

models_beatable.why: The question is moot: the existing models (DeepPROTACs 2022 and later DC50/Dmax predictors) address small-molecule degraders, a different modality, and this data cannot train a competitor in either modality.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition - there is no baseline model for antibody-based GPCR degraders to run, and no feature/label table to run it on.

ml_idea: The idea considered was: predict degradation potency (how far the receptor level drops, and at what antibody concentration) from the bispecific antibody's design - which receptor-binding arm, which transferrin-receptor-binding arm, valency, and arm geometry - using ESM-2 embeddings of the antibody arms plus categorical design features. It is dead on arrival here because the designs number in the tens, their sequences are not in the open deposit, and the potency values exist only as unfitted dose-response blocks inside GraphPad Prism figure files.

effort.compute_note: Size is trivial (6 MB). The 40-hour estimate is for reverse-engineering GraphPad Prism's internal sheet format across 375 panels, re-fitting dose-response curves, and hand-mapping panel titles to constructs - and it would still yield only tens of labelled designs. Not timed, estimated from the archive structure I inspected.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the distinct antibody constructs that have a measured potency value. I did this by listing the 375 Prism sheet titles: they are figure panels covering roughly five receptors and a few dozen constructs, which kills the project in one command.

verdict_reason: Part A fails at A2, A3 and A5. The Zenodo deposit is honest, open and complete figure source data (I opened all 6 files), but it is 375 GraphPad Prism figure panels plus one cardiac-contractility spreadsheet - there is no potency column, no antibody sequences, and the number of distinct engineered designs is on the order of tens rather than the ~1,500 rows a model needs. This is an excellent wet-lab paper and a non-candidate for machine learning.
